title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) comparing an LLM‑only generation pipeline to a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All planned pairs completed: every initial candidate passed the validator, so no repairs were invoked (baseline = 200/200 passes; GVR = 200/200 passes). Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank under the frozen shared‑initial generation policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, deterministic execution accounting, the preregistered Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements in the recorded contamination summary, and a focused discussion of methodological tradeoffs, threats to validity, and operational implications.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises productivity gains in network operations (NetOps) but raises safety concerns: incorrect or semantically incompatible changes can cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validators, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, whether an automated GVR pipeline materially reduces validator‑detectable unsafe changes—beyond what a given generator and prompting policy already avoids—depends on baseline failure prevalence, validator coverage, and repair effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question to isolate this margin: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Our contributions are (1) a sealed, preregistered paired experiment design that fixes the generator output per task (shared‑initial) to isolate the marginal effect of validation+repair; (2) a complete execution and analysis bundle demonstrating deterministic accounting and the observed null outcome (no validator failures); and (3) an artifact‑grounded discussion of methodological tradeoffs and operational recommendations for evaluating GVR in practice.
sections.related_work: Large surveys and empirical studies document that large language models (LLMs) produce factual errors and are sensitive to prompt design and sampling, motivating verifier‑assisted and grounding approaches to improve reliability. Prototype NetOps work shows feasibility of intent→configuration translation but often lacks instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate studies. Architectural proposals and prototype systems combine LLMs with deterministic validators or emulators to improve safety; red‑team audits and recent agentic‑AI analyses highlight configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection attacks that can alter safety outcomes. Our work is situated within this line of research by providing an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic repair on a fixed-model, fixed‑sampling policy. Representative references supporting these points include surveys of LLM behavior, intent→configuration prototypes, and verifier‑assisted architectures (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study was preregistered (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) as a paired design with n = 200 tasks. For each task we produced one deterministic initial generation that was reused for both conditions (LLM‑only baseline and GVR guarded). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline with an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Confidence intervals were obtained by bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration fixed a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task and a maximum model‑call cap of 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs). The paired, shared‑initial design intentionally removes sampling variance so the paired contrast isolates the marginal effect of validating and (if necessary) repairing an identical generator output.

Task bank, validator, and holdout. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration task bank with 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge). Each task encodes an initial and expected final state plus workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields) and a required sequence. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect possible validator blind spots at the data‑plane level; results from that holdout are summarized in the analysis contamination summary.

Determinism and sampling reconciliation (reviewer request). The preregistration specified deterministic shared‑initial generation semantics (sampling intention: temperature = 0). During execution, model_configuration.json records "temperature": null; this null value does not reflect the adapter‑enforced semantics. Determinism was enforced by the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter such that a single shared initial candidate was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions for each task. Evidence for enforced single invocations is present in the execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation artifacts (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts indicating shared_initial_generation = 200). These adapter/provider accounting fields—recorded in the execution bundle—establish that exactly one deterministic shared initial generation per task was used in the paired comparison. We therefore reconcile the apparent configuration field inconsistency by reporting that adapter enforcement (not the model_configuration.json temperature field) produced the observed shared‑initial deterministic semantics; supporting accounting artifacts are archived with the run.

Mininet holdout seed and reproducibility disclosure (reviewer request). The Mininet 10% holdout contamination detector executed as preregistered and the contamination summary reports zero disagreements. We disclose a reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the 10% Mininet holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle. This omission prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of which tasks comprised that holdout despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements. We highlight this gap in Methods to make clear the scope and limits of the contamination check.

Repair policy and handling. When the primary validator reported violations the preregistered policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM; any repaired candidate was re‑validated. Pairs with both conditions failing due to infrastructure errors were to be excluded by deterministic rule; pairs flagged for validator–emulator disagreement were to be excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered contamination plan. All such handling rules and their deterministic application are described in the preregistration and logged in the execution manifest.

Statistical implementation. Primary inference used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 paired table (n11, n10, n01, n00) produced by the paired analysis executor. Bootstrap percentile CIs were computed over 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) to characterize the paired difference distribution. Secondary/exploratory analyses (preplanned) included logistic regressions and descriptive summaries for repair iterations and model‑call cost; these were executed only when relevant data were generated.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes and pairs. Model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were used. Completed_pair_count = 200 and there were no technical failures affecting the primary analysis. Adapter/provider accounting confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, consistent with the shared‑initial design.

Validator outcomes and paired contingency. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test returns p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent under the frozen shared‑initial policy, the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction could not be meaningfully evaluated on this sample.

Repair and contamination outcomes. No validator failures were observed; consequently the repair branch was never invoked and secondary estimands related to repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failures, and model‑call costs for repair remain unpopulated for this run. The preregistered Mininet 10% holdout contamination check (20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements per the contamination summary; however, as noted in Methods, the explicit seed for the holdout draw is not present in labeled artifacts, which limits exact reproducibility of which tasks were emulated.

Representative diagnostics. Representative validator traces (archived per‑task) show that required_command_count values matched parsed_command_count and that validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true with violation_count = 0 for examined examples. Difficulty annotations in the task bank indicate the benchmark contained nontrivial workflow constraints (labels such as "medium", "hard", "very_hard" and patterns like make_before_break_uplink_switchover and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change), demonstrating that the task set exercised dependency checks even when outputs satisfied the validator.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The observed null (no validator‑detected failures) is an artifact‑grounded empirical outcome under the chosen model, prompt policy, and the paired shared‑initial design. The exact p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] are mathematically correct in the degenerate case of zero discordant pairs and indicate no margin for the preregistered McNemar test to detect an effect. This outcome does not imply that GVR is universally unnecessary; it implies that, for this workload and generation policy, there were no validator‑detectable failures for the repair mechanism to correct.

Methodological tradeoffs. The paired shared‑initial design isolates the marginal effect of validation+repair on an identical generator output, increasing internal control but excluding benefits achievable by re‑sampling the LLM. If an operational evaluator seeks unconditional failure rates or expects diverse failing draws, a different design allowing independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws (and nonzero temperature sampling) is preferable. Similarly, the one‑repair budget here constrains repair pathways; multi‑step repair or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation might produce different outcomes when initial failure prevalence is nontrivial.

Validator coverage and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators codify a checkable subset of intended constraints; they can still miss device idiosyncrasies detectable only by richer emulation or testbeds. The zero disagreements observed in the 20‑task Mininet holdout increase confidence that validator verdicts aligned with the emulator for that sampled subset, but the missing labeled holdout seed prevents exact reconstruction of that draw and therefore limits the strength of generalization from the holdout result. Larger emulation samples, multiple validators, and adversarial probing are recommended to reveal validator blind spots.

Operational implications. Before investing in automated repair, practitioners should (1) measure baseline validator failure prevalence under the intended generator/prompt policy, and (2) assess validator completeness via emulation or selective device checks. If baseline failures are rare, single‑pass automated repair yields limited marginal returns for validator‑detected errors; resources may be better allocated to improving validator fidelity, adversarial testing, or adopting multi‑sample generation policies to surface latent failure modes. If baseline failures are nontrivial, appropriately budgeted GVR can reduce validator‑detected errors; experiment design choices (sampling, repair budget, multi‑step repair) determine effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent under the frozen shared‑initial generation policy. The artifact‑grounded outcome demonstrates that GVR’s marginal measured value depends on workload and generator sampling choices. Future confirmatory work should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity and emulation coverage (with recorded holdout seeds), evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution artifacts, accounting, and analysis outputs are archived under the preregistration id cited in the Disclosure Statement for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). The experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired shared‑initial design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; adapter/provider accounting recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, which demonstrates that a single shared initial generation per task was enforced by the adapter despite a null temperature field in model_configuration.json. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Mininet emulation: a Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the contamination summary artifact reports zero disagreements for that holdout. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. No post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax and intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
